title: Book 8 opens: still brother-love; Exod 22 calf/sheep theft
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK EIGHT. Still concerning the love toward the brothers, and against the one who steals a calf or sheep.

Cyril: From every side then already, O Palladius, it is present for you to understand that the ancient law also commands that the words of the mystagogy be made both upright and exceedingly exact. And setting the matter as not without penalty for those accustomed to deceive some of the simpler ones, he said again: ‘And if someone should steal a calf or a sheep, and should slaughter or sell it, he will repay five calves instead of the calf, and four sheep instead of the sheep. And if the thief should be found in the dig-through, and having been struck should die, there is no murder for him; but if the sun should rise upon him, he will be liable, he will be killed in return. And if it should not exist for him, let him be sold instead of the theft; and if the theft should be caught and found in his hand, from donkey even unto sheep, alive, he will repay them double.’
notes_covered: title still brother-love + thief of calf/sheep
translator_notes: OET; Pass A≠B; mid-sentence PG cuts kept where present.

title: Calf/sheep = faithful flock; thieves sell souls to Satan; night vs sunrise
english: Palladius: The word is not very clear. But you, try to tell me what it is that is somehow oracularly spoken as in a riddle.

Cyril: The law usefully defines a penalty of the one wanting to grasp more, and somehow reins in the unbridled toward desire of whatever the neighbor or brother might happen to have, so that even if it should happen, he says, that the one condemned for this should die in the very act of stealing, no blame is rubbed onto those who have killed him. And he also dishonors him by saying that it is fitting to sell him if he cannot hold out toward payment of ransom, driving him with terrors unto needing to choose to live well. But the hidden mind of the history would be much other than this, and we must also say it as well as possible. Calf then and sheep, both pure and holy, and brought up to God unto a smell of fragrance. But the calf is in superiority and greatness of body; the other not so. For the sheep is less than a calf. Calves then and sheep as somehow pure and most holy animals are the holy multitude of those justified through faith, and splitting the hoof and bringing up rumination according to the law, and workers of cultivated fruits; for the calf works the ground; and the sheep also is fruitful, and the flock of the called has been shut into the divine courts, that is, in churches; and very many are the thieves around it, digging through and slipping in, and by manifold deceits drawing out the souls of the simpler ones, and all but selling them down to the destroying Satan; yet the one who has done something such will repay five calves, he says, instead of one, and four sheep instead of the sheep; for fivefold upon the calf is the judgment for the one who has stolen, and fourfold must come upon one sheep, he says, according somehow, I think, to the measure of the spiritual quantity according to virtue of those who are being destroyed, having set the punishment. And the bodily would be a type and shadow of the quantity in virtue; for the greater or less in fair dealings is easy to see among those who have believed, since not all are by chance in equality; ‘But each of us has his own gift from God, one thus, another thus.’ And if still stealing and digging through, and fulfilling the works of robbery, he should be caught as in night and darkness, he says, then let him also have died; and the matter is not murder, nor a charge against the doer. For the one who fell is grasping and violent, and has been wounded by the law of war; but when the sun has risen, and the time of the robbery has already passed, it restrains the hand of the one striking, and defines a murder-charge of the daring. For as long as the intelligible thief damages the soul of the one who has believed unto Christ, and draws it out from love unto God, if he should be caught in the very wrongs, he would suffer not unjustly also the need to have died; for he killed a soul, the better than body; but when the sun has risen also for him according to mind, and true knowledge is shining as in the order of light and day,
translator_notes: §2 ends mid-sentence (PG column cut); continues in §3.

title: Sunrise = knowledge/repentance; sell unrepayable; soul-trafficking death
english: Cyril: …he does not allow to be in danger, for the works of night and darkness are punished, but the things as in light thereafter no longer. And God has justified release from the ancient charges, and from those in ignorance and darkness. And indeed let it also be said to those who have arrived from sin unto the intelligible light, ‘You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.’ Thus the Lord has also justified the divine Paul, who was formerly a blasphemer and persecutor and insolent man; for beyond measure he persecuted the Church of God and was laying it waste.
Palladius: You have spoken most excellently.

Cyril: And if he should not be able, he says, five calves instead of one, and four sheep instead of one, let him be sold instead of the theft. You see how the law clearly writes down the slavish dishonor of those who have continuous and unwashed-out sin, and who are not even able, so to speak, to beat off the charges with ransom, both through weakness of resolve not enduring to sweat unto repentance, and through the labors unto this to propitiate God? So he says very well that they are to be sold. For he does not allow those so polluted to be numbered among those freed through the divine grace. And being thrust out from the honor fitting for free persons, they also will hear: ‘Behold, you were sold for your lawless deeds.’ And if he should be caught having stolen, he says, but not yet having destroyed—that is, if someone of those accustomed to think otherwise should be caught having begun deceit and trickery unto others, but not yet having conquered and brought the hearers down unto destruction—he will repay double. For the master of the flock will take back what is his own, and the buffoon will also be required to give accounts; for this would be the thing in the double; and he will endure the penalty unto death. For what he wished to do unto others, he himself would suffer, and very fittingly.

Palladius: How truly destructive and altogether terrible is the matter of the deceivers, concerning whom I think somehow Christ himself also foretold: ‘Take heed from those who come toward you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are rapacious wolves.’

Cyril: Rightly then the law adjudges that every such one must have died as of wild beasts. For it has been written in Exodus: ‘If someone should steal one of the sons of Israel, and having overpowered him should sell him, and he should be found in him, let him die by death.’ And in Deuteronomy: ‘And if a human should be caught stealing a soul from his brothers, the sons of Israel, and having overpowered him should sell him, that thief will die.’ For it is not lawful that the holy race in Christ be laid waste, and be brought down somehow into an unfamiliar slavery by those accustomed to do this; for just as those who deceive boys separate them from city and households, and sending them out from free persons’ boasts, bring them under the yokes of forced slavery; in the same way, I think, those who lead away those who have chosen to think uprightly, and who practice the life fitting for free persons, onto

title: No greeting to heretics; virgin/betrothed laws quoted (Exod/Deut)
english: Cyril: …what seems most mindless to themselves, carrying them off by intricate deceits of thoughts, will fittingly endure the charge of robbery upon human souls; and the penalty for them is death. To such ones, ‘Do not even say Welcome,’ says the disciple of the Savior, not training us unto savagery of manners, but because the sheep is not suited unto dispositions with the wolf; and those accustomed to think otherwise are somehow incompatible with one another; ‘For what portion has a believer with an unbeliever?’ And in addition to these things, the divine Paul writes that one must not be intertwined with the fornicators of this age. So that then some may not be snatched as from a paternal hearth—the Church of God—and be carried off into churches of those doing evil, selling down as it were their own mind by turnings unto baseness—‘For bad associations corrupt good characters’—the law defines death as the judgment for those who have most unholily desired to do this. And you would see the law hinting the same to us sideways again, and through another oracular saying. For it orders worldly matters unto what has uprightly, through the more manifest and ready contemplation for those who wish to grasp it. For we will not abolish the history among the things most useful as stale. For even the letter itself will sometimes benefit the hearers, and it somehow travails in depth the spiritual things, and has the power of the thinner thoughts as in fine shadows. And he said again in Exodus: ‘And if someone should deceive an unbetrothed virgin, and should sleep with her, he will dowry her with a dowry for himself as wife. And if refusing he should refuse, and her father should not wish to give her to him as wife, he will repay silver to the father according as is the dowry of the virgins.’ And somehow widening the divine commandment for us, the divine Moses says in Deuteronomy: ‘And if a human should be found sleeping with a woman cohabiting with a husband, you will kill both, the man sleeping with the woman, and the woman, and you will remove the evil from the sons of Israel. And if there should be a virgin betrothed to a man, and a human finding her in a city should sleep with her, you will lead both out upon the gate of their city, and they will be stoned with stones and will die; the young woman, because she did not cry out in the city, and the human, because he humbled the wife of his neighbor; and you will remove the evil from yourselves. And if in a field a human should find the betrothed woman, and having forced her should sleep with her, you will kill only the human who slept with her; and to the young woman you will do nothing; there will be for the young woman no sin of death, because as if a human should rise up against his neighbor and murder his soul, so is this matter, because he found her in the field, the betrothed young woman cried out, and there was no one to help her.’ The matter of the history then, I think, will somehow need no word for some to be able to understand; for it is very clear and evident.
translator_notes: Continues §3 mid-sentence; history clear before spiritual track in §5.

title: Soul wed to Christ; betrothed = catechumen; city vs field begins
english: Cyril: But we must, as it seems, having set these aside for the present, go the inward and hidden path.
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: I say then that just as among wrongs unto a woman the most grievous of all would be adultery, undoing another’s marriage and making a divorce of those already joined, in the same way, I think, among charges unto human souls the most impious and most unbearable of all is to practice the corruption not simply unto any chance soul, but unto the one already somehow cohabiting and united to Christ, the bridegroom from above and from heaven; for we are united to him both through the faith and further through having a share of holy Spirit; ‘For the one clinging to the Lord is one spirit,’ according to the Scriptures. So the law justly honors with death together with the adulterer also the woman who has fornicated—him as putting in the seeds of the impiety present in him, and her because, dishonoring the law of genuineness, she has become another’s, and opening her mind to his corruptions she received the pollution from human inventions.
Palladius: The word is persuasive.

Cyril: To a woman then, cohabiting with a husband according to laws, one must very well liken the soul cohabiting and united to Christ through faith and Spirit. And we will reckon as a betrothed virgin the one called unto beginnings of true knowledge, not yet wholly united to Christ, and still awaiting as somehow a marriage and a truer mode of joining the grace through holy baptism and the participation of the holy Spirit, having received as earnest and as beginning of converse the word of catechesis. Thus our divine mystagogue—Paul this is—brought the Church from the nations to Christ; for he writes thus: ‘For I betrothed you to one husband, to present a pure virgin to Christ.’ And the Bridegroom himself somehow says through a voice of prophets: ‘And I will betroth you to myself unto the age, in righteousness and in judgment and in mercy and in compassions; and I will betroth you in faith, and you will know the Lord.’ If then the charges of the corruption should come about, he says, also upon some such soul, let the matter be written as adultery; for the betrothed woman is under obligation, and already under the hand of the bridegroom after a little. But if the wrong should come about in a city, he says—that is, either in Christ’s Church, and in the city of the living God, which angels and holy men inhabit, leaders and teachers able to help those in danger and being deceived—let the suffering virgin also die together with the deceiver. For it being possible readily to flee the corruption, if she had reported to the teachers who know how to save, she sickened the suffering as voluntary, and does not have the leading-away unto the base from necessity. notes_covered: adultery of soul already united to Christ

title: Field without teacher; unbetrothed soul; heretics snatch Gentiles/Jews
english: Cyril: …the city of the living God, but somehow in a field and in a countryside, where there was no helping mystagogue, and much emptiness of those accustomed to persuade unto the better, and the deceit as in scarcity of pedagogues, let only the one who forced be in danger; for the deed is already grasping, and a suffering without help, and a necessity somehow hard to flee will turn aside the charge; or shall we say it is not superfluous to blame those upon whom things have been brought unwillingly as involuntary?
Palladius: Altogether so; for the law is holy.

Cyril: You speak well; and it makes the examination of the deeds thinner, and somehow measures the angers to the wrongs, neither releasing altogether the lesser wrong from needing to be punished, nor setting it in equality with what is beyond this, but somehow turning the motion equal-sized to the charges. For he said again: ‘And if someone should find the virgin girl who has not been betrothed, and having forced her should sleep with her, and it should be found, the human who slept with her will give to the father of the young woman fifty didrachms of silver, and she will be his wife, instead of those things for which he humbled her; he will not be able to send her away for all time.’ So adultery made the one joining with a betrothed woman liable, according clearly to the modes already said. And if she should appear, he says, still unjoined, and not yet pledged to Christ through the faith, as a soul in the form of a virgin, and then someone should be caught having defiled her with words unto impiety, and having led her aside from wandering unto wandering—such a thing as heretics do, sometimes snatching those from the nations and from Jews, and persuading them to follow themselves—he will find the attempt not without penalty. For he will repay to the Father of spirits—that is, to God—the accounts of the wrong, the penalty being very well typed as in a loss of money. And ‘She will be his wife’ is useful to the history.
Palladius: I understand what you say; for the law is double—fleshly and spiritual.

Cyril: And observe how not even the word of the ancient commandment was ignorant of what Christ said concerning man and woman: ‘What therefore God has yoked, let a human not separate.’ For let her be his wife, he says, instead of those things for which he humbled her; he will not be able to send her away for all time. And in addition to this, consider how high as in boasts is the height of all-holy virginity; for the word of the God-inspired Scripture both knows and thinks fit to name as humiliation the taking-away of virginity, and as it were the putting-off of solemnity.
Palladius: You have spoken uprightly.

Cyril: Having then declared as God-hated and truly unholy the deceit of the otherwise-thinking, and the turning unto baseness of those accustomed to corrupt those who have chosen to walk uprightly, and the leading-away onto what it does not fit

title: Idle word-fights; pregnant struck; faith as embryo; Galatians travail
english: Cyril: …he has also invented something other, which the divine Paul himself also made for us a most excellent of lessons, saying: ‘Not to word-fight upon nothing useful, or upon overturn of the hearers.’ For superfluous dialogues, and the contentious altogether about inquiries, generate fights not necessary, and strike the mind of the hearers; for some, from lightness, sometimes receive readily and ignorantly what is not upright and said, and are eager to praise it; and others, bringing the more shameful vote upon the best things, having sickened the equal lack of education with the others, would be caught; and altogether few are those who know how to discern, and to set what benefits before what is naturally harmful. And these barely keep the mind unstruck in the word-fights of the others. So that the matter will not be without penalty for those wanting to do it, the law again hints to us, saying: ‘And if two men should fight, and should strike a woman having in belly, and her child should come out not yet formed, he will be fined with a fine, according as the husband of the woman should lay on, and he will give with dignity. And if it should be formed, he will give soul instead of soul.’ A word then: in the womb the embryo is barely seen human-formed, and goes into a type of the body according to us then, when also a number of a fortieth day is completed upon it. For this very reason they say that Moses the all-excellent, somehow travailing and reshaping Israel from the wandering in Egypt unto the life in law, abstained from foods and drinks; ‘For bread,’ he says, ‘I did not eat, and water I did not drink forty days.’ And unto us ourselves one must suspect that Christ both did and endured this. For in him the nature was reshaped unto sanctification through self-control, having from unbridled appetite in beginnings in the first-formed sickened the pollution unto sin and transgression. These things it is not unpersuasive for us to think; yet however the word of the history may somehow hold, let it be set aside now; but how it would be fitting to understand that a woman having in belly is struck by those accustomed to word-fight—come already, come, let us examine; for to speak very thinly in these things is not unpleasant. So a fruit and conception of mind would be the faith unto Christ, reshaping us unto him through complete knowledge, and forming us into a divine type; and indeed those who have believed through a voice of Isaiah, marking this somehow, I think, have cried out very well: ‘Through your fear, Lord, we received in belly, and we travailed, and we bore, we made a spirit of your salvation upon the earth.’ So a fruit and spiritual and saving conception of mind would be the faith unto Christ, which also seals the divine characters in us. To those then who from more perfect knowledge have flowed ignorantly unto the lesser and more incomplete—Galatians these are—the divine Paul was addressing, saying: ‘My little children, whom I again travail, until Christ should be formed in you.’ For having begun in spirit, the
translator_notes: Continues §6; ends mid-sentence into §8 Galatians flesh-completion.

title: Formed faith = soul-murder if aborted; beast-torn; mixed seed/vineyard
english: Cyril: …completion according to flesh they were practicing, having been transferred unto the worship of the law; for this very reason they were also making the formation of Christ in themselves incomplete, somehow aborting the good lying in themselves as in a womb. So the perfect in knowledge and the unmixed unto faith will house the formation of the Savior in the souls of all of us, and this in us will be as somehow a divine sowing. Whenever then some should be scandalized as from the word-fight of certain ones; and then the soul that has suffered this should abort the faith and knowledge lying as in travails and treasured within unto mind—if it should be, he says, not yet formed, that is, if still incomplete and less beautiful, the cause of the scandal will altogether and in every way endure a penalty, which the bridegroom of this one should lay on, he says—that is, Christ; and he will give with dignity, that is, let him also confess grace, not having undergone the penalty unto complete destruction. And if the intelligible conception of the soul should be formed, he says—that is, if there should be knowledge and faith of Christ wearing formation—he will be subject to the accounts concerning the last things, as already also a murderer. For death of soul is the putting-off of the blameless faith, and the loss of knowledge that holds rightly. Therefore he says that needing to share unholy teachings, and whatever words a man would make, having become devilish prey, and somehow food of the herd of demons, is a pollution; and he forbids again, saying as in a riddle, ‘And flesh taken by beasts you will not eat; throw it to the dog.’ For it is custom of the divine Scripture to name as dog the shameless and unclean human. And every word somehow foul and stinking would be fitting for such a one, I think, and composed from Beelzebul himself, as of a wild beast having eaten down the soul that fell under him and serves unto this; ‘For no one says, Anathema Jesus, except in Beelzebul.’ And for holy ones to come into participation of thoughts and words so shameful or adulterated is altogether unfitting. ‘For there is no communion of light toward darkness.’
Palladius: Truly.

Cyril: And that it is fitting for those allotted to lead, and leaders of flocks, to stay awake, he again oracled. And what manner of our fairness unto this would become, he hints, saying in Leviticus: ‘You will not make your cattle mount with a differently yoked animal, and you will not sow your vineyard with different seed.’ For to herds of goats and sheep, or indeed to a vineyard, one must very well liken the multitude under hand. For the divine Peter heard: ‘Simon of Jonah, do you love me? Feed my lambs, shepherd my sheep.’ And concerning those from Israel, the prophet Isaiah was saying: ‘For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel, and

title: Shepherd keeps flock pure; bestiality type of alien teaching; slaves next
english: Cyril: …a human of Judah, a beloved newly planted.’ So a virtue of a shepherd is not to let loose upon sheep some animal of another form, so that they fall under somehow foreign mountings, lest it bear something of another nature, and having bent away from the natural good birth present in it; and the caretaker of vineyards, if he should be sensible and have practiced farming most excellently, would never endure the dry of the seeds to grow under the vines themselves, lest, the moisture being spent for them unto the alien, they themselves fall short concerning what is their own. Come then already somehow from an image now unto the spiritual: let us not allow the rational flocks to be led unholily under the sowings of the otherwise-teaching—intelligible ones clearly, and the introductions as in word; for the fruit from dissimilar resolve is very ugly, and the words of those not of like faith would become providers of base conceptions for those who have received them; and we being vineyards, and lying in the order of orchards, it is somehow fitting to be crowned with single-formed fruit, and to decline the double-natured mode. For there is no word unto natural likeness for wheat and clusters. So let there be for none of us a place of alien seeds.
Palladius: You speak well.

Cyril: And in another way also he shows the differently mannered as unjoined and incompatible, and split from communion toward one another, having set beside as a type the most outlandish and altogether strange joining of the rational animal toward what is not such, but of another form and out of tribe. And indeed he also says in Exodus: ‘Whoever should sleep with a beast, you will kill him by death.’ And more clearly again in Leviticus: ‘And whoever should give his lying in a four-footed animal, let him be put to death by death, and you will kill the four-footed; and a woman who should approach unto every beast to be forced by it, you will kill the woman and the beast; let them be put to death by death; they are liable.’ For converses and as it were intelligible mixings and joinings toward those for whom it would least be fitting, and for whom the mind has sickened unto unreason the last, are providers of death, both for those who corrupt and for those who endure the corruption as voluntary.
Palladius: Most uprightly and very holily the law speaks.

Cyril: And you would still marvel also at this; for there were somehow some who, as from unbearable grasping, even if they should not wish to endure the corruption from uprightness of thoughts unto what holds sideways, also somehow from necessity, perhaps not without tears, suffer the wandering. So the law did not think fit to overlook even such a race as without help.
Palladius: What sort of thing do you mean?
Cyril: The one bound tight with a yoke of slavery and held down by the authorities of those who have bought them.
notes_covered: Exod/Lev bestiality as type of illicit joinings
translator_notes: Continues Isaiah from §8; slave eye/tooth relief in §10.

title: Slave eye/tooth → free if soul harmed; leave masters who lead into error
english: Palladius: And in what manner then has the law also helped these?

Cyril: For it loosens from bond and necessity, if the harm should be about soul, and it has clearly justified that the wronged may run off if he should wish, nothing tripping him. For he said thus sideways in Exodus: ‘And if someone should strike the eye of his house-slave, or the eye of his maidservant, and should blind it, he will send them out free instead of their eye; and if he should cut out the tooth of his maidservant, or the tooth of his house-slave, he will send them out free instead of their tooth.’ As far as concerns outward contemplation and a ready mind, it checks the boldness, and makes the angers of the owners measured, and does not wish to go as far as those things through which the subordinated would come to be the loss unto being well. And it nowhere allows the things from passion to go unbridled, and already to be practiced unto the nature itself, of which the Creator alone would be understood as existing Master; for slavery and the suffering upon it is not a natural sickness, but brought in from grasping. In Christ then God and Father reshapes the whole nature at once unto what was in beginnings. ‘For if someone is in Christ, a new creation.’ And the shame of slavery is altogether taken away; for Paul writes that ‘In Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free.’ And for the present the law, training on toward the perfect, takes away the unbridled of the authority, and what is beyond the measure of what is fitting, setting as penalty for those who slight the law the release of the wronged. But these things unto letter and shadow, if someone should also choose to understand this way; and if the aim of the law should be interpreted spiritually, you would also strike, O Palladius, in another way the contemplations in it; for this worldly light we receive and marvel at with the eyes of the body; but the divine and intelligible light rises in our hearts; and the food of the body is ground with teeth, and the matter will be a path unto life; but the things of the divine contemplations, hard and hard to reach, are all but crushed with the strength of the understanding as with a tooth, and feed a soul. And indeed Wisdom, opening for us the divine and spiritual table, ‘Come, eat my bread,’ she says. So even if harm should somehow befall a house-slave concerning some of such things, a master going astray and forcing him to slip from uprightness of dogmas unto outlandish wandering, let the bond be loosed, he says, and let there be no word of a necessary yoke. And let the terror of the authority also be thrown somewhere, and let the yoked one go thereafter wherever the unharmed holding would be found for him; for nothing was better than soul. And in order that he may save, he says, let him have been released from slavery. And you would see the word true, and still being fulfilled in times according to us; for house-slaves do not endure masters who lead them unto wandering, having nobly withdrawn from the authority hung over them
notes_covered: leave masters who force dogmatic error
